items.title: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, regulation 13: Capabilities and training
items.quote: the introduction of new technology into the employer’s undertaking
items.why: The only general UK duty found that links capability to new technology: employers must take employees' capabilities into account when entrusting tasks and train them when new technology exposes them to new risks. Limited to health and safety.

items.title: Human factors: Training and competence
items.quote: There should be refresher training for infrequent, complex or safety critical tasks and this may include appropriate reassessment
items.why: The regulator's principle that competence must be maintained by practice and reassessment, including for rare and emergency tasks. Written for major-hazard industries, not for AI; the page shows no publication date. The page shows no publication date; 2026 is the year it was read.

items.title: CAA Paper 2004/10: Flight Crew Reliance on Automation
items.quote: there is a risk that flight crew no longer have the necessary skills to react appropriately
items.why: The UK precedent from the sector that met this problem first: reliance on automation, loss of manual flying skills and poor monitoring. Written by Cranfield University for the regulator. Aviation, 2004; cited as an analogy.

items.title: Safety Alert for Operators 13002: Manual Flight Operations
items.quote: continuous use of autoflight systems could lead to degradation of the pilot’s ability to quickly recover the aircraft from an undesired state
items.why: A regulator turning the finding into practice: operators should create opportunities to exercise manual skills in line operations and training. The model for a retained-capability decision. Advisory, not binding. The FAA site refuses the automated checker (HTTP 403); this entry is re-read by hand at each review.

items.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
items.publisher: Hao-Ping (Hank) Lee and others, Carnegie Mellon University and Microsoft Research (CHI 2025)
items.quote: you deprive the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgement
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation, where the authors restate Bainbridge's 1983 'ironies of automation' (the original is paywalled and was not read). Survey of 319 knowledge workers: higher confidence in the tool went with less critical thinking. Self-reported, not a measure of skill loss.

items.title: How AI Impacts Skill Formation
items.publisher: Judy Hanwen Shen and Alex Tamkin (arXiv preprint 2601.20245)
items.locator: Abstract, page 1; results, page 2; section 4.3 for the sample
items.quote: AI-enhanced productivity is not a shortcut to competence
items.why: Source of the figure: 'a reduction in the evaluation score by 17%' for developers who learned a new library with AI assistance; 52 participants, 26 in each group. A preprint, not peer reviewed, by researchers at an AI developer; one task. It also finds that some ways of using AI preserved learning.

items.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
items.publisher: Nataliya Kosmyna and others, MIT Media Lab (arXiv preprint 2506.08872)
items.quote: We recruited a total of 54 participants for Sessions 1, 2, 3, and 18 participants among them completed session 4.
items.why: Widely cited on cognitive offloading. Read mainly to record its limits: a preprint, essay writing by students, and only 18 people in the final session. Not strong enough to carry a board-level claim alone.

items.title: The Future of Jobs Report 2025
items.quote: two-fifths (39%) of their existing skill sets will be transformed or become outdated over the 2025-2030 period
items.why: International comparator on how fast skills are changing, from an employer survey. An expectation, not a measurement, and about skills changing, not skills decaying.

items.title: Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers' awareness?
items.publisher: Brooke N. Macnamara and others, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (Springer, open access)
items.quote: we discuss how artificial intelligence assistants might accelerate skill decay among experts and hinder skill acquisition among learners
items.why: Peer-reviewed review by cognitive scientists setting out why AI assistance may speed the loss of expert skill, slow learners' acquisition of it, and hide both effects from the people concerned. That last point is why capability has to be tested and not assumed. Limits: the authors call it a 'theoretical perspective': it reasons from research on skill and automation and reports no new experiment; it says little research has yet measured the effect directly.

items.title: AI-induced Deskilling in Medicine: A Mixed-Method Review and Research Agenda for Healthcare and Beyond
items.publisher: Chiara Natali, Luca Marconi, Leslye Denisse Dias Duran and Federico Cabitza, Artificial Intelligence Review (Springer, open access)
items.locator: Abstract; section 2.1 for the systematic review method
items.quote: the erosion of medical expertise and the reduction of opportunities for skill acquisition due to AI-driven decision support systems
items.why: Peer-reviewed review (2025) of the evidence on loss of clinical skill from AI decision support. It separates two harms the criterion covers, experienced staff losing skill and juniors never gaining it, maps them to the competencies tested in the UK physicians' clinical examination, and calls for monitoring and long-run studies. Limits: medicine only; the systematic part rests on a small number of studies; the authors call for longitudinal studies and real-time monitoring, which do not yet exist at scale.

items.title: The Vicious Circles of Skill Erosion: A Case Study of Cognitive Automation
items.publisher: Tapani Rinta-Kahila and others, Journal of the Association for Information Systems, 24(5), 1378-1412 (AIS eLibrary)
items.locator: Abstract on the journal's own page
items.quote: Such skill erosion may remain obscure, acknowledged by neither workers nor managers.
items.why: The closest thing found to a study of the 'deskilling unnoticed' level in an ordinary business: an accounting firm whose staff lost expertise over several years of relying on software automation, which, the authors say, can go unacknowledged by workers and managers alike. They show how reliance breeds complacency in individuals and the organisation and weakens upkeep of competence. Limits: one firm; a case study in a peer-reviewed journal; software automation, not generative AI; only the abstract on the journal's page was read, not the full article.

items.title: Enhanced FAA Oversight Could Reduce Hazards Associated With Increased Use of Flight Deck Automation (Audit Report AV-2016-013)
items.publisher: U.S. Department of Transportation, Office of Inspector General
items.quote: to use and monitor automation systems while also maintaining proficiency in manual flight operations
items.why: An official audit finding that follows the two aviation sources already on the list: three years after the regulator's safety alert, the auditor found it could not tell how often pilots flew manually or whether airlines had acted. The lesson for a board is that advising people to keep skills up is not the same as checking that they do. Limits: United States; aviation; 2016; the report records the regulator's response, which was not followed up in this pass.

items.title: FCA Handbook, Training and Competence sourcebook, TC 2.1: Assessing and maintaining competence
items.quote: A firm must review on a regular and frequent basis employees' competence and take appropriate action to ensure that they remain competent for their role.
items.why: A binding UK rule that requires what this criterion asks: regular review of whether people are still competent, and action if they are not, with guidance that this covers technical knowledge, skills and expertise. It is the model for 'capability retention monitored'. Limits: financial services only, and only the retail activities the sourcebook lists; it does not mention AI or automation; the page says the section was last updated on 6 April 2026 and the rule itself is dated 21 March 2016.

items.title: GRI 404: Training and Education 2016
items.quote: This disclosure helps demonstrate how an organization works to monitor and maintain the skill sets of its employees.
items.why: The reporting standard under which an organisation would show the outside world that it keeps capability up: training hours per employee, programmes for upgrading skills, and the share of employees receiving regular performance and development reviews. It gives the 'monitored' and 'assured' levels a recognised form. Limits: voluntary; dated 2016; it measures training effort and reviews, not whether skills displaced by automation have been retained; it does not mention AI.

items.title: OECD AI Principles, Principle 2.4: Building human capacity and preparing for labour market transformation
items.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD.AI)
items.locator: Rationale for this principle, third paragraph
items.quote: skills development policies will need to focus on the distinctly human aspects necessary to complement AI systems, such as judgment, creative and critical thinking
items.why: International comparator. The intergovernmental AI standard names the capabilities that have to be kept as AI spreads: judgement, creative and critical thinking and interpersonal communication. It gives a board a starting list for 'what stays human'. Limits: addressed to governments, not firms; non-binding; about skills policy in general and silent on skill decay from use of AI; the page carries no date (the OECD's principles page says they were adopted in 2019 and updated in May 2024).

items.title: Managing technology that manages people: November 2025. A Social Partnership approach to algorithmic management systems in the Welsh public sector
items.publisher: Welsh Government (guidance agreed by the Workforce Partnership Council)
items.locator: Section 'Due diligence and consultation during buying or building systems'; general principle 4 (Building capability)
items.quote: broader risks like work intensification, loss of expertise and overriding human judgment
items.why: UK government guidance that names loss of expertise as a risk to be assessed before a workplace AI system is bought or built, alongside a standing commitment to build capability at every level of the workforce. It is the only UK official text found that treats deskilling as something to assess in advance. Limits: devolved public sector in Wales only; guidance, not law; covers systems used to manage workers; it does not say how the risk should be measured.
